layers.description: These firms make engineered parts such as drivetrain, electronics, wiring and braking systems for vehicle makers. Contracts are linked to vehicle platforms and sold in bulk to a few large buyers. Margin depends on technical content, the buyers' bargaining power and raw material pass-through.

Tyre makers manufacture tyres sold to vehicle makers and to the replacement market through dealers. Replacement demand is steadier and priced better than original-fit supply. Margin is set by natural rubber and crude-linked input costs, and by brand and pricing power.

These companies design, assemble and sell cars and SUVs through dealers. They earn from vehicle sales, with mix and brand deciding realisations. Margin is set by scale, commodity costs, model mix and capital spent on new platforms and electric vehicles.

These firms build motorcycles and scooters sold through dealers and exported. Demand tracks rural incomes and urban commuting needs. Margin is set by scale, premium mix and commodity costs, and electric entrants face heavy capital needs.

These companies build trucks, buses, light commercial vehicles, auto-rickshaws and electric buses, earning from vehicle sales to fleet operators and transporters. Sales follow freight activity and replacement cycles; this layer is set apart by commercial-use vehicles.
Non-bank lenders financing purchases of commercial vehicles, cars and tractors. They earn interest spread and fees.
Companies making storage batteries or agricultural tractors and machinery, sold to farmers, fleets and consumers rather than as vehicle parts.

layers.description: These companies make the chemical and fermentation-based molecules that go into medicines. Margins depend on process efficiency, scale and long-term customer contracts. They are also shaped by capital-intensive plants, competition from imported ingredients and government support for local production.

These firms develop and make molecules for innovator clients and are paid per project or under supply contracts. Margins depend on scientific skill, client stickiness and plant utilisation. Regulatory track record matters more than price in winning work.
Margins depend on the number of competitors per product, the scale of first-to-market launches and regulatory inspection outcomes. Heavy buyer concentration in the US limits pricing power.

These firms sell branded medicines through medical representatives to doctors and then via chemists in India. Margins depend on brand loyalty, field force productivity and the share of products under national price control. Imported ingredient costs affect input prices but pricing is more stable than exports.

These companies develop and sell copies of biologic drugs, which need cell-line work and clinical trials. Margins depend on regulatory approvals, partnerships and very high capital spending. Few competitors and complex manufacturing can support pricing once approved.

layers.description: These platforms market and sell policies from many insurers to customers, mostly online. They earn commissions rather than bearing claims risk. Margin depends on commission rates set by insurers and by regulation, and on customer acquisition cost and renewal persistence.

Life insurers sell long-term protection, savings and annuity policies and invest the premiums. Margin depends on product mix, persistency, expense control and investment returns. Regulation of charges and commissions and tax rules on policies also shape profit.

General insurers sell motor, fire, travel, marine and commercial cover on annual contracts and reprice often. Margin depends on claims experience, pricing freedom, commissions and catastrophe losses. Government-regulated tariffs in some lines and investment income on float also matter.

Specialist health insurers sell individual and group medical policies and manage hospital claims. Margin depends on medical cost inflation, network pricing, fraud control and annual premium repricing. Regulatory limits on premium hikes and claim settlement rules affect pricing power.

Reinsurers take on portions of risk from primary insurers in return for a share of premium. Margin depends on how well large losses are priced and on global reinsurance rates. Capital strength and policy-linked cessions from Indian insurers support the business.

layers.description: These plants electrolyse salt or process limestone and brine to make caustic soda, chlorine and soda ash sold in bulk. Margins are set by power cost, plant utilisation and import prices, so earnings are cyclical. Capital intensity is high and pricing power is limited.

These companies convert petrochemical and aromatic feedstocks into products such as phenol, acetone and nitro-aromatics sold to other manufacturers. Margins depend on the gap between crude-linked feedstock and product prices, and on imports. Integration with feedstock helps but pricing power stays modest.

These firms process fluorspar-derived inputs into refrigerant gases, fluoropolymers and fluorinated intermediates. Margins rest on handling hazardous chemistry, product approvals and refrigerant regulation and quotas. Capital needs are high, and some raw materials are imported.

These companies make agrochemical and pharma molecules to a customer's specification under multi-year supply contracts. Margins depend on process know-how, customer approvals and the pace at which customers launch products. Contracts give some pricing protection but customer concentration is high.

These firms make niche products such as additives, surfactants, dyes and pigments in smaller volumes for specific uses. Margins rest on product approvals, technology and switching costs for customers. Pricing power is stronger than in bulk, though raw materials are partly imported.
